summaries.Q821009: Headquarters of the European Commission, at the junction of the rue de la Loi and the boulevard Charlemagne. Lucien De Vestel designed its cross-shaped plan, with four unequal wings that do not rest on the ground but hang from a central core on steel ties. Evacuated in 1991 for asbestos removal, it was reoccupied in 2004.
summaries.Q55123016: Motorised sheet metal sculpture by Alexander Calder, made in 1958 for a pool of water in front of the American pavilion at the Brussels World’s Fair. It is Calder’s only monumental piece created for a Belgian site. Forgotten, then long kept in store, it was restored and unveiled on the rue Montagne de la Cour on 21 June 2000.
summaries.Q945059: This federal scientific institution has its seat in Cinquantenaire Park and brings together several sites: the Art and History Museum, the Halle Gate, the Musical Instruments Museum housed in the former Old England store, and the Museums of the Far East in Laeken, closed to the public since 2013.
summaries.Q2671145: Art nouveau mansion designed by Victor Horta for the industrialist Armand Solvay, at 224 avenue Louise. The permit was issued in 1895, the shell finished in 1898, the furnishing carried on until 1903. The architect drew everything, down to the furniture. Listed in 1977, world heritage in 2000, it has been open to visits since 2021.
summaries.Q1101790: Laid out on a former parade ground for the fiftieth anniversary of Belgian independence, in 1880, it is arranged around a triple arch whose plans were drawn by Charles Girault, inaugurated in 1905 and topped by a bronze quadriga. The Royal Museum of the Army, Autoworld and the Royal Museums of Art and History surround it.
summaries.Q2086424: Former Cistercian nunnery founded at the source of the Maelbeek, suppressed and sold as national property in 1796. Most of the buildings date from the 18th century, when the abbesses rebuilt the complex in the French style: main courtyard, monumental staircases, terraced gardens. The Gothic church is now a parish church.
summaries.Q7740434: Functionalist tower on the boulevard de Waterloo, designed by Henri Montois and Emmanuel Gran, built from 1963 to 1967 and opened under the name Brussels Hilton. It is 99 metres high, has 30 floors and overlooks the Petite Ceinture and the place Louise. The hotel’s success took it from 308 to 431 rooms.
summaries.Q2217006: In the heart of the Marolles district, this square, laid out at the same time as the rue Blaes, holds a flea market every day: in 1873 the council decided to move the junk market from the place Anneessens there. It stands on the site of a locomotive works, part of whose cellars survive under the square.
summaries.Q421992: Complex of European Parliament buildings, in the Léopold district. The Paul-Henri Spaak building, which the people of Brussels nicknamed the “Caprice des Dieux” after the cheese box, holds the hemicycle under a cylindrical glass roof. The official seat remains the Louise-Weiss building in Strasbourg, where plenary sessions are held.
summaries.Q55616349: Bronze statue by Tom Frantzen showing Jacques Brel with his arms open to the crowd, a pose he liked to take on stage. Prompted by a request from the traders’ association of the place de la Vieille Halle aux Blés, it was unveiled on that square on 11 October 2017, a few steps from the Fondation Brel.
summaries.Q2277238: Car museum housed in the south east hall of the Palais du Cinquantenaire, under a metal frame and glass roofs. More than 300 vehicles are shown, among them Minervas and limousines that belonged to the royal family. The museum was founded in 1986 at the initiative of Charly De Pauw, around the collection of Ghislain Mahy.
summaries.Q1818182: Victor Horta built this Art nouveau mansion in three phases from 1895 for Edmond van Eetvelde, on the avenue Palmerston. The facade shows its metal structure; inside, an octagonal rotunda is crowned by a stained glass dome on eight slender steel columns. It has been on the Unesco world heritage list since 2000.
summaries.Q1865794: Urban ensemble stepped between the royal quarter above and the city centre below. It brings together the Royal Library of Belgium, the General State Archives, the Square congress centre and a garden designed by the landscape architect René Pechère. At the top stands The Whirling Ear, a sculpture by Alexander Calder.
summaries.Q3586107: Catholic church in Roman Byzantine style, place de la Reine in Schaerbeek, on the royal route running from Laeken to the Royal Palace of Brussels. Its octagonal plan, by Louis van Overstraeten, draws on San Vitale in Ravenna. Opened for worship in 1853 and consecrated in 1902, it was closed in 1966, then restored and reopened in 1996.
summaries.Q2580013: Historic bar on the rue des Alexiens, in one of the few 17th century houses to have survived the bombardment of Brussels. It was a haunt of artists, the surrealists first of all but also the Cobra movement: René Magritte, Hergé and Jacques Brel went there. The decor, listed since 1997, can no longer be altered.
summaries.Q1049291: This neoclassical square, laid out by the engineer Claude Fisco under the name place Saint-Michel, was renamed on 2 October 1830 in memory of the fighters of the Belgian revolution: 467 of them are buried under the paving, around the monument sculpted by Guillaume Geefs. Facades and monument have been listed since 1963.
summaries.Q1816400: Standing in Saint-Gilles not far from the Bruxelles-Midi station, from which it takes its name, it reaches 150 metres without the spire, making it the tallest tower in the country. Its 37 floors hang from a central core holding the stairs and lifts: the method avoids columns and frees large usable spaces.
summaries.Q16509720: This eclectic group stands in the middle of the place du Luxembourg, in Ixelles, in memory of the industrialist John Cockerill and of steel workers. Unveiled in 1872, it repeats the monument raised in Seraing by Armand Cattier. Four bronze workers stood at the corners of the pedestal; the statue of the mechanic Beaufort was taken down in 2024.
summaries.Q256200: The museum occupies the former mansion of the patron Henri Van Cutsem, avenue des Arts, whose interior Victor Horta transformed from 1890 to 1893 to display the collections, keeping the neoclassical shell. The sculptor Guillaume Charlier inherited it in 1904 and left the house in 1925 to the commune of Saint-Josse-ten-Noode.
summaries.Q28485845: This eclectic palace, built to plans by Léon Suys, was finished in 1873: Greek cross plan, dome, abundant sculpted decoration to which Auguste Rodin contributed. The lions on the staircase tell the market, head up for a rise, back bent for a fall. Restored from 2020 to 2023, it houses an exhibition on beer.
summaries.Q1704088: The park lies in the valley of the Josaphat stream, whose name is said by tradition to come from a pilgrim back from the Holy Land struck by the likeness of the place to the valley of Josaphat, near Jerusalem. Opened to the public in 1904 on four hectares, it now covers twenty: ponds, lawn, municipal greenhouses and sculptures.
summaries.Q535244: Of the former great beguinage of Brussels, whose last houses disappeared in 1856, only this church remains. The baroque building, whose first stone was laid in 1657, stands on the foundations of the Gothic church destroyed during the religious troubles: hence its Latin cross plan, unusual for the baroque.
summaries.Q551479: On the place de la Monnaie, the neoclassical facade of the opera house, designed by Louis Damesme, dates from 1819; the fire of 21 January 1855 left only the four walls standing, and Joseph Poelaert rebuilt the theatre almost identically. In 1830 a performance of La Muette de Portici set off the riot that led to the Belgian revolution.
summaries.Q2706608: Laid out in 1777 among the four streets around the Parc de Bruxelles, it was called rue de Brabant until 1797. It links the rue Royale to the avenue de la Joyeuse Entrée by way of the Robert Schuman roundabout and runs past buildings tied to the European institutions, among them the Berlaymont. “16, rue de la Loi” stands for the Prime Minister.
summaries.Q2636175: Tower block on the place Madou, along the small ring road, in Saint-Josse-ten-Noode. This 32 storey building was put up from 1963 to 1965 to plans by Robert Goffaux, who drew on the MetLife Building in New York. A renovation grafted a triangular volume onto the front and two floors at the top, taking its height to 120 metres.
summaries.Q16665229: Commissioned in 1911 from the sculptor Thomas Vinçotte, finished only in 1921 because of the First World War, this semicircular monument in Euville stone commemorates the explorers, missionaries and soldiers of the colonisation of the Congo. On a side group the word “arabe” was chiselled off, restored in 1992, then erased again.
summaries.Q2869992: Built in 1905 by Paul Cauchie for himself and his painter wife Lina, this house on the rue des Francs serves as a sign for their talent: a render coats the facade like a canvas and carries sgraffito; a caryatid with raised arms holds the cartouche “Par nous, pour nous”. It is open to the public on Saturdays.
summaries.Q2429651: At no. 8 place du Petit Sablon, the palace was home to the Egmont family, whose Lamoral was executed on the Duke of Alba’s orders in 1568, then to the Dukes of Arenberg in the 18th century. Fire ravaged it on the night of 22 to 23 January 1892. Sold to the City of Brussels in 1918 and to the State in 1964, it houses the foreign affairs ministry.
summaries.Q1073360: Four ponds formed by the course of the Maelbeek originally covered the territory of Ixelles. Two remain: the upper pond, born of the joining of the Pennebroeck and the Ghévaert, and the lower pond, a remnant of the Grand Étang that covered the place Flagey. The site has been listed since 1976.
summaries.Q2762071: Built around 1125 for the merchants’ quarter, near the small port on the Senne, the church stands next to the palais de la Bourse, hence its nickname Saint-Nicolas de la Bourse. Its choir extends the central nave at an angle and small houses built against it hide its side facades. A cannonball from 1695 is lodged in a pillar of the nave.
summaries.Q3495665: Ground of the Royale Union saint-gilloise in the parc Duden, in Forest, the stadium was inaugurated on 14 September 1919 with a gala match against the Milan Club. The stand building, put up in 1926, shows an Art deco facade 101.40 m long, with seven panels sculpted by Oscar De Clerck. This facade is listed.
summaries.Q3432642: Starting from the place Royale, it runs along the Parc de Bruxelles, passes the Congress Column and runs straight to the porte de Schaerbeek. Its first section was laid out between 1776 and 1780 by the architect Guimard. With the rue des Palais and the avenue de la Reine it forms the royal route from the Royal Palace to the château de Laeken.
summaries.Q3533638: This tower block was raised between 1968 and 1983 at the crossing of the boulevard du Jardin Botanique and the rue Royale, on the site of the former porte de Schaerbeek. It housed the Belgian finance administration and is part of the Cité administrative de l’État. A heavy renovation upset its structure between 2005 and 2008.
summaries.Q377500: The institution brings together six museums: Oldmasters, Magritte, Wiertz, Meunier, Fin-de-Siècle and Modern Art, that is some twenty thousand paintings, sculptures and drawings. The building on the rue de la Régence is by the architect Alphonse Balat. The Fin-de-Siècle museum has been temporarily closed to the public since January 2024.
summaries.Q842660: Housed in the house and studio of Constantin Meunier, in Ixelles, bought by the State in 1936, the museum opened to the public in 1939. Around 150 drawings, paintings and sculptures trace the period 1875-1905, marked by the artist’s social awareness. Since 1978 the museum has been part of the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium.
summaries.Q1131821: Residence of the dukes of Brabant, then of the Burgundian, Spanish and Austrian sovereigns, the palace was ravaged by fire on the night of 3 to 4 February 1731. Its ruins were cleared between 1774 and 1778 to make way for the place Royale district. Only the underground parts remain, open to visits from the BELvue museum.
summaries.Q2423861: The Société royale de Zoologie bought this pleasure estate in 1851 and had it laid out as an English style park by Alphonse Balat and Louis Fuchs, before setting up a zoological garden there. The city of Brussels took the estate over in 1877. It holds the Museum of Natural Sciences and the European Parliament’s Paul-Henri Spaak building.
summaries.Q1903443: Built on a filled in dock of the old port, it replaces an older church of which only the tower survives. Joseph Poelaert drew the plans and ran the works from 1854 to 1859; his pupil Wynand Janssens took over, and the inauguration took place on 6 October 1874. Gothic forms and Renaissance decoration are mixed there.
summaries.Q2285837: Designed by Victor Horta at the initiative of the banker Henry Le Bœuf, the Art deco building was put up between 1922 and 1929 on the slopes of the Coudenberg; its height had to be cut so as not to block the view from the Royal Palace. The Henry Le Bœuf concert hall, underground, seats 2,200. The palace signs its activities with the Bozar brand.
summaries.Q2523530: Laid out around 1865, at the same time as the covering of the Senne and the making of the central boulevards, it owes its name to the palais de la Bourse, which takes up its south east part. Under the square lie the ruins of the former Recollects convent. It was an important place of remembrance after the attacks of March 2016.
summaries.Q152072: This fountain takes the form of a bronze statue 55.5 centimetres tall showing a naked little boy urinating. It stands in a rocaille stone niche dating from 1770, at the crossing of the rue de l’Étuve and the rue du Chêne. The statue on the spot is a copy; the original is kept at the Brussels city museum.
summaries.Q1995367: Between 1898 and 1901, on the rue Américaine, Victor Horta built his house and his studio: two buildings conceived together but each keeping its own identity, to separate private life from work. The staircase is not shut in a shaft, it forms the backbone of the house, whose centre is lit by a skylight. The museum opened in 1969.
summaries.Q19974092: This museum of the National Bank of Belgium traces the history of money, from barter to euro coins and notes. The collection holds more than 24,000 notes and coins covering more than 2500 years. The eclectic building was put up from 1872 to 1874 for the Union du Crédit, to plans by the Brussels architect Désiré De Keyser.
summaries.Q14505682: This neo-Gothic building stands on the north side of the Grand-Place, facing the town hall, and houses the Brussels city museum. A bread hall came before it, mentioned as early as 1321. The 16th century Gothic building, left unfinished, was demolished then rebuilt by Pierre-Victor Jamaer, who added the central tower planned from the start.
summaries.Q739334: This park in Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, at the corner of the rue Royale and the boulevard du Jardin botanique, occupies the site of the botanical garden created in 1826. The plants left for Meise from 1940 and the park was redesigned to plans by René Pechère, just in time for Expo 58. The greenhouses hold a cultural centre, Le Botanique.
summaries.Q3527925: Built in 1782 to plans by Louis Montoyer, this 540 seat theatre borders the Parc de Bruxelles, facing the federal Parliament, and shares the site of the former Vauxhall with the Cercle Gaulois and the Vauxhall bandstand. At first an annexe of the Monnaie theatre, it was given over to shows by young actors, a kind of drama school.
summaries.Q3390534: 350 metres long and 70 wide, this gently sloping square runs between the rue Ducale and the rue Royale; the Parc de Bruxelles borders it to the north, the Royal Palace to the south. It owes its name to the Royal Palace and the palais des Académies, and has borne it since 1827. The national day parade, on 21 July, is usually held there.
summaries.Q152360: A naked little girl squatting and urinating, this bronze statue about 50 cm tall stands at the end of the impasse de la Fidélité, in the Îlot Sacré district. A female counterpart to Manneken-Pis, it was created in 1985 by Denis-Adrien Debouvrie and unveiled to the public in 1987. People throw coins into its basins.
summaries.Q46012: Wanted by the European Parliament, this museum opened to the public in 2017 in the Eastman building in the parc Léopold, a former dental clinic designed by Michel Polak and opened in 1935. The permanent exhibition takes up four floors and some 4,000 m2, in twenty-four languages. Admission is free.
summaries.Q488688: Drawings, paintings, studies and sculptures by Antoine Wiertz (1806-1865) are gathered on the rue Vautier, in Ixelles, in the studio that was also the home of this Belgian romantic artist from 1853 until his death. The museum is a section of the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium.
summaries.Q2616099: Built from 1823 to 1828 by Charles Vander Straeten and Tilman-François Suys, this neoclassical building stands east of the place des Palais, at rue Ducale 1. Home of prince William of Orange, it was sequestrated after 1830, given to the Belgian State in 1842, assigned to the Museum of Modern Painting in 1860, then to the Academies in 1876.
summaries.Q3363922: This public park of about 2 hectares, in Ixelles, is a former private arboretum. The dendrologist Jean-Louis Semet, owner in the early 1950s, enlarged the garden with neighbouring plots and turned it into an arboretum with his gardener Hector Noyer between 1953 and 1980. Spared by housing schemes, the park opened to the public in June 1985.
summaries.Q2957320: Built on the foundations of an earlier sanctuary, some two hundred metres south of the Grand-Place, this small Gothic chapel keeps a Brabantine Gothic part dating from the 15th century. The cutting of the North-South rail link razed the district: it is the only building on the north side of the rue de la Madeleine to have escaped.
summaries.Q1973948: Two concert halls, the main one and Le Club, make up this cultural institution of the Flemish Community, boulevard Anspach. In 1912 the place was a fairground hall called the Vieux Düsseldorf; the name Ancienne Belgique appeared in 1932, with the Mathonet family. Renovated from 1993, the hall reopened in 1996.
summaries.Q2385288: A road and transport hub in Saint-Josse-ten-Noode, the square opens onto the rue Neuve. The gare du Nord stood there until the mid 1950s, before it was moved several hundred metres north; the Rogier international centre, built on its site in 1960, was demolished in 2001. The square was redesigned from 2008 to 2017.
summaries.Q205064: This bronze dog by Tom Frantzen lifts its leg against a bollard, at the corner of the rue des Chartreux, set into the paving of the pavement since 1999. Commissioned by the local committee in the spirit of the zwanze, the sculpture is a nod to Manneken-Pis. In Brussels dialect, zinneke means the little Senne and a mongrel dog.
summaries.Q815542: The comic strip museum occupies, on the rue des Sables, the Art nouveau building designed by Victor Horta in 1906 for the Waucquez fabric store. Restored from 1984 to 1989, the place has housed the centre since 6 October 1989. A permanent exhibition traces the history of the comic strip.
summaries.Q2261451: This former store on the Mont des Arts takes up partly a neoclassical building, partly an Art nouveau annexe by the architect Paul Saintenoy: iron columns and beams, faience friezes, turret and canopy. Old England left the premises in 1972; renovated from 1989, the building houses the musical instruments museum.
summaries.Q2480190: Gustave Strauven designed this Art nouveau house, built between 1901 and 1903 on the square Ambiorix for the painter Georges de Saint Cyr. On a facade barely four metres wide rises a scaffolding of cast and wrought iron interlace, each balcony having a different railing. Listed in 1988, it was restored between 2009 and 2019.
summaries.Q269654: Dedicated to Saint Michael and Saint Gudula, the collegiate church was raised to co-cathedral of the archdiocese of Malines-Brussels in 1962. Work on this Brabantine Gothic building began with the choir in 1226; the facade dates from the years 1470-1485. Its two towers, attributed to Jan Van Ruysbroeck, are unfinished and were to carry spires.
summaries.Q2617482: This parish church of the Marolles district, rue des Minimes, stands in the upper part of the centre. Built from 1700 to 1715 on a basilica plan, it belongs to a transitional style, the end of Brabantine baroque and the start of classicism, with a modest bell tower to the right of the facade. Its organ is the oldest in Brussels.
summaries.Q3527923: This entertainment theatre in the Royal Galleries of Saint-Hubert was opened in 1847. Destroyed in 1951, it was restored by the architect Paul Bonduelle and the designer Stéphane Jasinski: the hall keeps its Italianate look of red and gold velvet and its 850 seats now face the stage. The ceiling carries a cloud fresco by René Magritte.
summaries.Q3076025: This high flow drinking water fountain stands at the corner of the rue des Pierres and the rue du Marché au Charbon, in the centre of Brussels. It was inaugurated in 1704, but the name of its sculptor remains unknown.
summaries.Q1736784: Interlaced arms hold a globe in the colours of the European flag; the whole is topped by a dove of peace. More than 5 metres high, this polyester resin statue by Bernard Romain was made under the artist’s direction by children with visual impairment. It stands in the square Van Maerlant.
summaries.Q1395176: Federal museum taking up the northern half of the Cinquantenaire museum complex, that is 40,000 square metres of exhibition space. Its collection grew out of a military history section shown at the World’s Fair of 1910; it reached the site from 1923. The Air hall, designed by Gédéon Bordiau, holds more than 100 aircraft.
summaries.Q635307: Working and reception place of the King of the Belgians, who lives at the château de Laeken. The building, in front of the Parc de Bruxelles, faces the palais de la Nation. Two Austrian mansions joined under William I form its core; Léopold II had the facade redone to plans by Henri Maquet. It is open to visits from 21 July to the end of August.
summaries.Q941560: Art nouveau mansion built from 1903 to 1904 for Édouard Hannon, at the corner of the avenue Brugmann and the avenue de la Jonction. It is the only Art nouveau work by his friend the architect Jules Brunfaut. The corner bay carries a bas-relief by Victor Rousseau, La fileuse. Now a museum, it is called Maison Hannon.
summaries.Q1548310: Raised in 1897 for the international exhibition, this oriental pavilion in Moorish style, by Ernest Van Humbeeck, held a panoramic canvas of Cairo designed by Émile Wauters; the attraction closed in 1963. King Baudouin gave it in 1967 to the king of Saudi Arabia and the mosque was inaugurated in 1978. The minaret, unstable, was wrapped in 2025.
summaries.Q3584899: At 136 avenue Dailly, in Schaerbeek, the building replaces a first church dedicated to Saint Alice, a Cistercian nun who died of leprosy at La Cambre abbey. Building began in 1952 to plans by Willy Van Hove; cardinal Van Roey laid the first stone in 1953 and his auxiliary bishop Suenens consecrated the church in 1954.
summaries.Q215429: The bombardment of August 1695 by the French troops of marshal de Villeroy ruined the square: only the facade and the tower of the town hall and a few stone walls were spared. The houses were richly rebuilt in stone by the guilds. The present facades come from the restorations carried out at the initiative of Charles Buls.
summaries.Q51056992: The sculptor Henri Lenaerts showed the burgomaster Charles Buls seated on the stone bench around the fountain, a book in hand, a dog nibbling his sleeve, rather than on top of a pedestal. The statue looks towards the Grand-Place. In 2019 the basin had too many cracks for the fountain to be turned on.
summaries.Q2859916: Wanted by Léopold II for the fiftieth anniversary of Belgian independence, the monument long stayed unfinished: in 1897 only the vertical piers of the arch designed by Gédéon Bordiau had been built. In 1904 the French architect Charles Girault redrew a triple arch, raised in eight months by 450 workers and inaugurated on 27 September 1905.
summaries.Q943581: A section of the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, housed in a neoclassical building on the place Royale and opened to the public on 2 June 2009. The collection, the richest in the world devoted to Magritte, brings together more than 150 works; the route, chronological and thematic, covers three floors and starts with the last.
summaries.Q1255327: Sole medieval remnant of the Grand-Place, facing the Maison du Roi, this Gothic building went up in the 15th century in three stages by different architects: hence the asymmetry of the wings framing the tower, eleven arcades on the left, six on the right. Its spire bears a copy of Martin Van Rode’s Saint Michael; the original is at the city museum.
summaries.Q2628206: Bought in 1756 by the governor Charles Alexander of Lorraine, this former mansion of the Orange-Nassau family was enlarged around 1760, probably by Jean Faulte, with a wing of summer apartments and a semicircular entrance court decorated with allegories of good government. More than three quarters of the palace were demolished in the 1960s.
summaries.Q763565: Former chapel of the Blessed Sacrament of the Miracle, built in 1455 rue des Sols, dismantled for the Central Station, then rebuilt rue van Maerlant, where it reopened for worship in 1908. Bought by an association of European civil servants, it was consecrated on 25 September 2001 as an ecumenical place with stained glass by Thomas Reinhold.
summaries.Q1491935: Galerie du Roi, galerie de la Reine, galerie des Princes: three covered passages designed by Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar, the oldest pedestrian precinct in the city. Léopold I laid the first stone on 6 May 1846, the opening took place on 20 June 1847. The two main galleries, 8.30 metres wide, carry a glass roof 18 metres up.
summaries.Q1049313: Neoclassical square of 77 m by 113 m, built between 1775 and 1782 where the Coudenberg palace had burned in 1731. The statue of Charles of Lorraine that stood there was pulled down by the French, put back, then torn down and melted; the centre stayed empty for long, until the equestrian statue of Godfrey of Bouillon by Eugène Simonis, in 1848.
summaries.Q3553062: Sculpture by Tom Frantzen set up in 1985 on the square Sainctelette, in Molenbeek-Saint-Jean. It shows a Brussels policeman caught by a “scamp of the canal” coming out of a sewer. The artist meant to depict “youth making authority totter”.
summaries.Q222297: Natural history museum and research centre, on the edge of the parc Léopold, rue Vautier. Created by royal decree in 1846, it moved to the heights of the park between 1889 and 1891 and opened to the public on 22 July 1891. Its highlight remains the Bernissart iguanodons, found in 1878 in mine galleries, in Hainaut.
summaries.Q850537: Seat of several courts and tribunals, this eclectic building of Greco-Roman inspiration is the work of Joseph Poelaert and covers 26,000 m2 of ground. The first stone was laid in 1866, the inauguration took place on 15 October 1883, after the architect’s death. The dome, burned in 1944, was restored from 1948.
summaries.Q3145619: Art nouveau building put up from 1894 to 1898 for the lawyer and documentalist Paul Otlet, by Octave Van Rysselberghe, with Henry van de Velde signing the interior decoration. Its two asymmetrical facades, in golden Savonnières stone, meet at a corner oriel. Listed in 1984, it houses a law firm.
summaries.Q2002492: A chapel dedicated to the Virgin, raised by the Grand Serment of crossbowmen, was finished in 1318. The arrival in 1348 of a statuette held to be miraculous drew the devout, and the offerings paid for a new sanctuary in the 15th century, whose choir was finished in 1435. The flying buttresses were added at the end of the 19th century.
summaries.Q2166044: Raised in 1872-1874 by Antoine Trappeniers for the Caisse générale d’épargne et de retraite, the building was bought in 1891 by the Wielemans-Ceuppens brewery, then turned into a luxury hotel by Alban Chambon and opened in 1895. The first Solvay Congress was held there in 1911. Closed since April 2020, it is due to reopen after renovation.
summaries.Q1821749: Created after the covering of the Senne (1867-1871), it bears the name of Charles de Brouckère, burgomaster of Brussels. It lies in line with the boulevards Émile Jacqmain and Adolphe Max to the north and the boulevard Anspach to the south. Part of the central pedestrian precinct since 2015, it has been repaved and given water jets.
summaries.Q27476493: This eclectic monument was raised in 1897 in the middle of the place de Brouckère, in tribute to the burgomaster Jules Anspach, promoter of the covering of the Senne and the central boulevards. Taken down in 1973 for the metro, the fountain was put back only in 1981, its upper part alone, between the quai aux Briques and the quai au Bois à brûler.
summaries.Q2988142: Built in 1381, the Halle Gate is the last remnant of the second medieval wall of Brussels, the only survivor of its seven gates: its successive uses, among them as a prison, saved it from demolition. Henri Beyaert gave it its neo-Gothic castle look from 1868 to 1871. The museum traces the history of the building and of the city.
summaries.Q1881679: Victor Horta built this mansion from 1892 to 1893 for his friend Émile Tassel, a professor at the Université libre de Bruxelles. The first synthesis in the world of Art nouveau in architecture, it was declared world heritage by Unesco in 2000. The facade mixes white stone and metal; the interior can be seen only on a guided tour.
summaries.Q15939973: Raised from 1776 to 1781 to plans by Barnabé Guimard, this neoclassical pavilion belonged to the set meant to shape the place Royale. It owes its name to Philippe of Belgium, count of Flanders, third son of Léopold I, who bought it in 1866. Two added wings gave it its U-shaped plan. The Court of Audit sits there.
summaries.Q3109592: Built from 1776 to 1787, it is part of the neoclassical ensemble that forms the edge of the place Royale. Its facade with a triangular pediment and six Corinthian columns suggests a Greco-Roman temple. It was above the steps of the porch that Léopold I swore, on 21 July 1831, the oath that made him the first king of the Belgians.
summaries.Q3467613: Opened in December 2003 in the impasse de la Fidélité, near the Grand-Place, this bar is known for the range of its beer list: a month after it opened, the Guinness Book of Records recorded it as the establishment offering the most beer brands in the world. The Jeanneke Pis statue is opposite.
summaries.Q1070882: One of the largest squares in the Brussels region, it was born in Ixelles from the draining of the northern tip of the Grand Étang. Long an open air car park, it was redesigned from 2003 and inaugurated on 5 July 2008. The former Maison de la radio, now Le Flagey, sets the tone of the surrounding architecture.
